title: Chess Move Validation
description: Implement complex chess rules: castling, en passant, pawn promotion, check detection via attack maps, and pin detection for legal move generation.

segments.text: Basic piece movement is straightforward — a rook moves in straight lines, a bishop diagonally. But chess has special rules that trip up implementations: castling requires neither the king nor rook has moved and the king doesn't pass through check. En passant is a capture that only works for one move. These edge cases are where bugs live.

Castling has five preconditions: the king hasn't moved, the rook hasn't moved, no pieces between them, the king isn't in check, and the king doesn't pass through or land on an attacked square. Track 'has_moved' flags per piece. For the attack check, compute all squares attacked by the opponent — if any overlap with the king's castling path, castling is illegal.

En passant: when a pawn advances two squares from its starting position, an adjacent enemy pawn can capture it as if it had only moved one square. This is only legal immediately after the two-square advance — on the very next move. Track the 'en passant target square' as game state. Reset it after every move. This is the most forgotten rule in chess programming.

When a pawn reaches the eighth rank, it must promote to a queen, rook, bishop, or knight. The player chooses. Under-promotion to a knight is sometimes optimal to deliver check. Your move representation must include the promotion piece type. The UI must prompt the player for their choice before completing the move.

A player moves their bishop, exposing their king to a rook attack from the opponent. This is an illegal move because it puts their own king in check. How do you efficiently detect that a move would leave the king in check?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you efficiently detect if a candidate move leaves your own king in check (pin detection)?

segments.text: An attack map is a bitboard showing all squares attacked by a side. For each piece, generate its attack pattern and OR them together. A 64-bit integer represents the board — bit N is set if square N is attacked. Checking if the king is in check becomes a single bitwise AND: king_position AND opponent_attack_map. If non-zero, the king is in check.

A pin occurs when moving a piece would expose the king to attack. Detection: for each piece of ours, temporarily remove it from the board and recompute opponent sliding piece attacks. If the king is now attacked along that line, the piece is pinned. Pinned pieces can only move along the pin line. This reduces the legal move set significantly.

Legal move generation: first generate pseudo-legal moves for each piece, then filter out moves that leave the king in check. For efficiency, detect pins first and restrict pinned piece moves to the pin line. When in check, the only legal moves are: move the king, block the check, or capture the checking piece. Double check means only the king can move.

Checkmate: the king is in check and has no legal moves. Stalemate: the king is not in check but has no legal moves — this is a draw. The difference is a single bit: is_in_check. Generate all legal moves. If the list is empty and king is in check: checkmate. If empty and not in check: stalemate. This check happens after every move.

Design the data model for a chess game that supports undo, replay, and PGN export. What state do you need to store per move, and how do you efficiently undo complex moves like castling and en passant?
segments.thought_prompt: Design a chess move data model supporting undo, replay, and PGN export. What state per move?

segments.text: Chess move validation requires handling special rules — castling, en passant, promotion — plus global constraints like check, pin, checkmate, and stalemate detection. Attack maps via bitboards enable O(1) check detection. Pin-aware move generation filters illegal moves efficiently. The complexity is in the edge cases — each special rule interacts with every other rule.
